If it does not, then it is false in every sense—“objectively” false.
In principle, this all sounds very satisfactory.
In practice, however, it is easy to see that there is no way to distinguish primary qualities from secondary ones.
Contemporary physics, for example, treats as primary only those qualities that can be measured in units of space, time, and mass or “weight.”
But suppose we are dealing with an apple that has both a particular spatial shape and a particular colour.
If we attend only to these two qualities, nothing tells us that spatial shape is “primary” and “objective,” while colour is “secondary” and subjective.
Every quality is given to us in exactly the same way through experience.

We can examine the qualities themselves for as long as we like, but we will never find anything within them that justifies dividing them into two groups, one of which is to be regarded as “real” and the other as merely “subjective.”
Critical empiricism therefore divides qualities into primary and secondary categories without basing the division on anything inherent in sensory qualities themselves.
If we look at the history of science, we can see that qualities were classified as “secondary” whenever people could not reach agreement about them.
Conversely, qualities that people could determine unanimously were attributed to reality itself and treated as “primary.”
Suppose, for example, that a sick customer complains to a healthy merchant that his honey tastes bitter, while the merchant insists that it is sweet.
There is no way to make the two of them “agree,” since in a sense both are subjectively right.

But if the dispute concerns the weight of the honey sold, it is easy to reach a result binding on both sides and therefore regarded as “objectively” true—that is, as corresponding to reality itself, or to one of its “primary” qualities.
In other words, critical empiricism accepts the sceptical criticism of naive empiricism.
When speaking about reality, human beings really do sometimes produce incompatible discourses between which no decision can be made.
But critical empiricism says that this merely proves that those particular discourses do not concern reality itself. They are purely “subjective.”
Scepticism goes wrong only because it fails to notice that there are other discourses between which a choice can be made and about which we can therefore speak of objective truth.
Suppose one person says that a certain apple is red while another sees it as orange.
There is no way to settle the dispute at the level of colour itself.

But if we say that “in reality” both people are referring to a wave-like motion of something—of the “ether,” for example—with a certain wavelength, then by measuring that wavelength we can determine the apple’s “real” colour.
Or, more precisely, we should say that the real apple has no colour at all. It merely reflects “light” of a certain wavelength, which one person calls red and another calls orange.
Once we see this, it becomes easy to notice how closely the solution proposed by critical empiricism resembles the one proposed by critical rationalism.
In both cases, a kind of identification takes place.
The critical rationalist reconciles competing myth-makers by saying that what existed “in the beginning” can equally well be called “Serpent” or “Sun,” although “in reality” it is neither.

Critical empiricism reconciles two people looking at the same apple by saying that what one calls “red” and the other “orange” is not really a colour at all, but some spatial form that can be named however we like, provided only that it is measured correctly.
But if the method of solving the problem is the same in both cases, then similar consequences must follow.
Empirical identifications impoverish the content of discourse in exactly the same way as rationalist identifications did.
And because true discourse is supposed to correspond to reality itself, critical empiricism, by impoverishing discourse, must also simplify reality.
The tendency to simplify and impoverish the reality under investigation runs through the entire history of science.

In our own time, this tendency has reached its extreme in the so-called theory of general relativity, which reduces all physics to geometry—as Descartes once tried to do—and seeks to express the whole of reality through one universal mathematical formula, the “global tensor.”
Taken to its limit, then, critical empiricism reaches the same result as the radical critical rationalism of Parmenides:
everything that is genuinely real is one and the same, while the immense qualitative diversity of being is merely a subjective illusion about which no genuine, objective knowledge is possible.
There is no doubt that the “empirico-critical” method of simplifying and impoverishing reality through identification has been enormously useful in advancing our knowledge of the natural world.
Without it, there would be no physical or chemical sciences, and none of the achievements that depend on them.
There can therefore be no question of simply rejecting this method.
But its philosophical inadequacy is equally undeniable, because it cannot lead to omniscience.

When physics begins to treat itself as philosophy—when it claims that the aspect of reality it studies is nothing less than concrete reality as a whole—it becomes just as absurd as Parmenidean “monism.”

Once physics turns itself into a philosophical worldview, it is forced to maintain that a human body, the food a person eats, the house they live in, the ground they walk on, the sun that shines on them, and in general the entire world revealed through sensory perception are nothing more than subjective illusions.
“Objectively,” or “in reality,” only qualityless “atoms” would exist—or perhaps only a “curvature of space,” and so on.

Even leaving aside the fact that no sane person is likely to accept such an idealist interpretation of the sensory world, this physical and chemical “philosophy” is unsatisfactory from the start because, like Parmenidean philosophy, it is completely unable to explain where the supposedly “illusory” richness and diversity of sensory qualities comes from.
However much we combine “atoms” or complicate a “curved space,” we will never obtain, for example, this beautiful red apple: sweet, juicy, and appetizing.
This defect, shared by critical empiricism and critical rationalism, was noticed long ago.
Everyone can see that the method of identification cannot exhaust everything human beings are capable of knowing.

What is less often noticed is that just as the extreme rationalism of “Parmenides” ends by sealing itself into silence, radical “scientific” critical empiricism ultimately does the same thing: it excludes articulated and meaningful discourse.
By continually simplifying reality, science inevitably reaches a point at which meaningful discourse is replaced by mathematical formulas.
“What exactly is this energy to which, according to you, the entire universe can be reduced?”
The physicist will almost certainly point to some integral. But they will never be able to say what it is using the ordinary resources of human speech.
A “relativistic” physicist working with “tensors,” which cannot be translated into ordinary human discourse, is in the same position.
And contemporary quantum physics has discovered that when we try to talk about its mathematical formulas, we immediately become entangled in blatant contradictions.

If we speak of the electron, for example, we must represent it at the same time as a kind of “wave” spread over an indefinitely large space and as a “particle” concentrated at a single point within that space.
So critical empiricism, just like critical rationalism, achieves its goal of eliminating contradiction from discourse only at the very moment when it collapses into silence.
The natural reaction to this defect in critical empiricism is the emergence of a new and equally “critical” form of empirical scepticism.
It keeps the basic distinction between primary and secondary qualities but draws a new conclusion from critical experience:
we can speak only about secondary qualities.
The “thing in itself”—Kant’s Ding an sich—that is, reality as it exists independently of us, together with its “primary” qualities, is completely inaccessible to knowledge.
We “know” only what is reflected in sensory experience, and only about this can we speak.
The truth of our discourses can therefore no longer be established by comparing them with reality.
We must consequently do one of two things:
either abandon the concept of truth altogether,
or look for a criterion of truth somewhere other than where critical empiricism had sought it.
Critical empiricism tries to avoid this sceptical conclusion, just as rationalism had done, by becoming what I would call reflective empiricism.

This third and final form of empiricism no longer emphasizes the division between primary and secondary qualities, since that distinction inevitably impoverishes objective reality and eventually leads to “mathematical silence.”
Reflective empiricism accepts that we can speak about reality using the ordinary resources of discourse.
But it also knows that discourses about reality can be either true or false because the semantic structure of a discourse may or may not correspond to the real structure of the reality it refers to.
And human beings can distinguish true discourses from false ones.
In this respect, reflective empiricism agrees with reflective rationalism, which had likewise recognized both true and false discourses and the possibility of distinguishing between them.
The difference is that reflective rationalism had admitted the existence of “self-evident” truths, whereas empiricism rejects that possibility.
In other words, if we merely compare coherent discourses with one another, we have no way of deciding which is convincing and true and which is not.
The truth of a discourse can be established only by comparing it with the reality it refers to.
Until this comparison has been made, a discourse must be regarded as neither true nor false.
It is neither an affirmation nor a negation of anything.
The path to genuine knowledge therefore consists of two essential stages.
The first is to produce a series of articulated, meaningful, and coherent discourses that are not yet convincing—or, more precisely, are merely “hypothetical.”
The second is to choose between them by comparing them with reality.
Those that fail to coincide with reality are rejected as false.
Those—and only those—that do coincide with it are finally accepted as true.
All this would be completely convincing if it were actually possible to compare our hypotheses with reality itself.
But, as critical empiricism has already shown, human beings can compare their discourses only with sensory experience, not with reality itself.
And sensory experience can seriously distort reality without giving us any way to distinguish a distorting experience from a non-distorting one.
There is therefore no way to determine whether a hypothesis is really true—that is, whether it corresponds to reality itself rather than merely to a sensory experience that may be distorting reality.
In other words, human beings can never get beyond the first stage of the road to truth.
The road points toward truth, but never actually reaches it.
At first sight, this brings us once again to complete scepticism.
The distinctive feature of reflective empiricism, however, is that it tries to escape scepticism by introducing the idea that hypotheses can be more or less probable.
If absolute and final truth is inaccessible to us, then all we can do is choose between different hypotheses.
By replacing less probable hypotheses with increasingly probable ones, we can approach this inaccessible truth indefinitely.
